## Hermetic manifest builds with `sandbox = "pure"`

The single setting that enforces hermeticity is `sandbox = "pure"`. On Linux it seals both the network and the host filesystem — only Git-tracked files are copied into a temporary build root.

Because a pure build cannot reach the network, any dependency fetching must happen in a prior `sandbox = "off"` stage. The pure stage then consumes only what that stage produced, with zero host or network access.

```toml
# .flox/env/manifest.toml

[install]
go.pkg-path = "go"   # or your actual toolchain

# Stage 1 — fetch dependencies (network allowed, host FS allowed)
[build.deps]
sandbox = "off"
command = '''
  go mod download
  mkdir -p "$out/pkg"
  cp -r "$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod" "$out/pkg/"
'''

# Stage 2 — compile (network blocked, host FS sealed, Linux only)
[build.app]
sandbox = "pure"
command = '''
  export GOPATH="$PWD/.gopath"
  mkdir -p "$GOPATH"
  cp -r "${deps}/pkg/mod" "$GOPATH/"

  go build -mod=mod -o "$out/bin/myapp" ./...
'''
version     = "1.0.0"
description = "My hermetically built Go app"
runtime-packages = ["go"]   # trim to only what's needed at runtime
```

The single field that enforces hermeticity is `sandbox = "pure"` in each `[build.<name>]` table. On **Linux** this blocks network access AND restricts the filesystem to Git-tracked files (copied to a temp directory). make.pkg-path = "make"

```toml
  mkdir -p $out/vendor
```

## Minimal Runtime Closure for a Flox-Built Go Binary

The problem: every package in the `toplevel` install group (including the Go toolchain) is pulled into the runtime closure by default. Fix it with `runtime-packages = []` in the build table — Go produces statically-linked binaries and needs nothing at runtime.

### Manifest

```toml
version = 1

[install]
go.pkg-path = "go"

# Stage 1: vendor modules outside the sandbox (needs network)
[build.deps]
sandbox = "off"
command = '''
  go mod vendor
  mkdir -p $out/vendor
  cp -r vendor/* $out/vendor/
'''

# Stage 2: reproducible compile — no network, no host tooling leaking in
[build.myapp]
sandbox = "pure"
command = '''
  cp -r ${deps}/vendor ./vendor
  go build -mod=vendor -o $out/bin/myapp ./...
'''
runtime-packages = []   # Go binary is statically linked; toolchain stays out
```

**If you use CGO** (and therefore link against glibc), add it back:

```toml
[build.myapp]
...
runtime-packages = ["glibc"]
```

### Commands

```bash
# Build both stages (deps first, then myapp — ordering is automatic via ${deps})
flox build

# Verify the runtime closure is just the binary (no go, gcc, etc.)
nix-store -q --references ./result-myapp
```

## The problem

Nix determines runtime closure membership by scanning binaries for embedded store path substrings. A Go binary built without special flags contains the full path of the Go toolchain (e.g. `/nix/store/…-go-1.22.x/…`) embedded in build metadata, so Nix pulls the entire toolchain into the closure.

Two Go compiler flags eliminate those embedded references:

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-trimpath` | Strips all absolute source/toolchain paths from the binary |
| `-ldflags="-s -w"` | Strips symbol table and DWARF debug info (also removes path refs) |
| `CGO_ENABLED=0` | Pure-Go binary — no C runtime dependency at all |

## Complete manifest

```toml
version = 1

# go is a BUILD-time dep only; the built artifact in $out
# will contain no references to the go store path after -trimpath.
[install]
go.pkg-path = "go"

[build.myapp]
command = """
  CGO_ENABLED=0 go build \
    -trimpath \
    -ldflags="-s -w" \
    -o "$out/bin/myapp" \
    ./cmd/myapp
"""
```

Replace `./cmd/myapp` with your actual main package path (or `.` for a single-package repo).

```toml
[install]
gbenchmark.pkg-path = "gbenchmark"
catch2.pkg-path = "catch2_3"

```

```bash
flox install gbenchmark
flox install catch2_3
```

```bash
flox show gbenchmark
flox show catch2_3
```

- The install ID on the left (`catch2`) is just your manifest's label; the `pkg-path` on the right is what Flox resolves against the catalog.
- If you need these only for testing/benchmarking and want to keep them grouped separately from your main compiler toolchain, add `pkg-group = "testing"` to both entries.
